edges.effect_quant: In a large randomized aftercare trial, mindfulness-based relapse prevention reduced later substance-use days and heavy drinking compared with relapse prevention and treatment as usual, while a women-focused residential trial found a significant delay to first marijuana use (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.98) but not broad benefits across every substance outcome.
edges.population: adults with substance use disorders receiving aftercare or residential treatment
edges.mechanism: Mindfulness-based relapse prevention teaches people to notice craving, stress, and affective triggers without reacting automatically. This may lengthen the gap between urge and use, reduce cue-reactivity, and improve relapse coping, but the size of effect depends heavily on substance type, treatment context, and continued practice.
edges.summary: The evidence supports mindfulness-based relapse prevention as a credible relapse-reduction strategy, but not as a universal fix. It appears most helpful for delaying or reducing some forms of return to use, while other recurrence outcomes show smaller or inconsistent gains depending on the population and comparator treatment.
edges.caveats: This edge is mixed because benefits vary by substance, treatment setting, and dose of mindfulness practice. Some trials show clear improvements in marijuana or heavy-drinking outcomes, whereas others do not show broad reductions across all substance-use endpoints.

evidence.citation: Skrzynski CJ et al 2023 J Stud Alcohol Drugs
evidence.notes: Comparing the Efficacy of Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention Versus Relapse Prevention for Alcohol Use Disorder: A Randomized Control Trial. Both groups improved, but heavy drinking days remained lower after treatment in the mindfulness arm.

evidence.citation: Bowen S et al 2014 JAMA Psychiatry
evidence.notes: Relative efficacy of mindfulness-based relapse prevention, standard relapse prevention, and treatment as usual for substance use disorders: a randomized clinical trial. MBRP lowered substance-use days and heavy drinking relative to comparators during follow-up.

evidence.citation: Amaro H et al 2021 Psychosom Med
evidence.notes: Mindfulness-Based Intervention Effects on Substance Use and Relapse Among Women in Residential Treatment: A Randomized Controlled Trial With 8.5-Month Follow-Up Period From the Moment-by-Moment in Women's Recovery Project. Marijuana outcomes improved, but broader substance-use recurrence outcomes did not all differ.

new_entities.name: Mindfulness-based relapse prevention
new_entities.description: A structured relapse-prevention program that combines mindfulness practices with cognitive-behavioral strategies for coping with craving and high-risk situations.

new_entities.name: Substance-use recurrence
new_entities.description: Return to problematic alcohol or drug use after a period of abstinence, treatment, or meaningful reduction.
